summary: Defines an extension of the TCP Selective Acknowledgement option, letting a receiver report duplicate segments it has received. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: When a TCP receiver gets a piece of data it already has, it can now say so in the acknowledgement it sends back, using the space that the SACK option already provides. That lets the sender work out whether it resent something unnecessarily, and adjust itself so it does not happen again.

subtitle: How a TCP receiver can use the SACK option to tell the sender which data arrived more than once.

tldr.problem: The SACK option tells a TCP sender which out-of-order blocks have arrived, but it says nothing when the receiver gets a segment it already has, so the sender cannot tell an unnecessary retransmission from a needed one.
tldr.mechanism: The document specifies that the first SACK block in an acknowledgement may be used to report the duplicate segment that triggered it, calling that a D-SACK block. No new option and no separate negotiation are needed.
tldr.outcome: A sender that understands D-SACK can detect replication by the network, false retransmits caused by reordering, retransmission timeouts caused by lost acknowledgements and early timeouts, which lets it adjust its duplicate-acknowledgement threshold and its timeout.

facts.label: Fast Retransmit reorder threshold
facts.value: More than 3 packets out of order

today: RFC 2883 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the SACK option defined in RFC 2018, and the sender-side responses it discusses are left to later experimental proposals.

sections.title: What the Extension Adds
sections.content:
The Selective Acknowledgement option defined in RFC 2018 is used by the TCP data receiver to acknowledge non-contiguous blocks of data not covered by the cumulative acknowledgement field. However, RFC 2018 does not specify the use of the SACK option when duplicate segments are received. This document specifies that use, for acknowledging the receipt of a duplicate packet. The term D-SACK, for duplicate-SACK, refers to a SACK block that reports a duplicate segment.

The document makes no changes to TCP's use of the cumulative acknowledgement field, or to the TCP receiver's decision of when to send an acknowledgement packet. It concerns only the contents of the SACK option when an acknowledgement is sent.

The extension is compatible with current implementations of the SACK option in TCP: if one of the TCP end nodes does not implement the D-SACK extension and the other does, the use of D-SACK by one of the end nodes will not introduce problems. The use of D-SACK does not require separate negotiation between a TCP sender and receiver that have already negotiated SACK capability. The absence of separate negotiation means the receiver could send D-SACK blocks when the sender does not understand the extension, in which case the sender will simply discard any D-SACK blocks and process the other SACK blocks in the SACK option field as it normally would.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new goes on the wire. The receiver just uses the first slot of an option it already sends, and an older peer that does not know the rule ignores that first block and reads the rest as usual.

sections.title: The SACK Option and Its Blocks
sections.content:
The SACK option as defined in RFC 2018 carries a number of SACK blocks, where each block specifies the left and right edge of a block of data received at the TCP receiver. A block represents a contiguous sequence space of data received and queued at the receiver, where the left edge of the block is the first sequence number of the block and the right edge is the sequence number immediately following the last sequence number of the block.

The option begins with a Kind field set to 5 and a Length field, followed by the left and right edges of the first block, then the left and right edges of the nth block. The edges are 32-bit sequence numbers, so each block occupies eight octets.

RFC 2018 implies that the first SACK block specifies the segment that triggered the acknowledgement: when the data receiver chooses to send a SACK option, the first SACK block MUST specify the contiguous block of data containing the segment which triggered this ACK, unless that segment advanced the Acknowledgment Number field in the header. However, RFC 2018 does not address the use of the SACK option when a duplicate segment is received. It specifies that each block represents received bytes of data that are contiguous and isolated, and that if sent at all, SACK options SHOULD be included in all ACKs which do not ACK the highest sequence number in the data receiver's queue. RFC 2018 does not specify the use of the SACK option when a duplicate segment is received, and the cumulative acknowledgement field in the ACK acknowledges all of the data in the data receiver's queue.
sections.plainLanguage: The option is a list of ranges of bytes the receiver already holds. Each range has a start and an end, and the end is one past the last byte. The first range normally describes the segment that caused the acknowledgement.

sections.title: The Rules for Reporting a Duplicate
sections.content:
When D-SACK is used, the first block of the SACK option should be a D-SACK block specifying the sequence numbers for the duplicate segment that triggered the acknowledgement. If the duplicate segment is part of a larger block of non-contiguous data in the receiver's data queue, then the following SACK block should be used to specify this larger block. Additional SACK blocks can be used to specify additional non-contiguous blocks of data, as specified in RFC 2018.

The guidelines for reporting duplicate segments are summarized as five rules. First, a D-SACK block is only used to report a duplicate contiguous sequence of data received by the receiver in the most recent packet. Second, each duplicate contiguous sequence of data received is reported in at most one D-SACK block: the receiver sends two identical D-SACK blocks in subsequent packets only if the receiver receives two duplicate segments. Third, the left edge of the D-SACK block specifies the first sequence number of the duplicate contiguous sequence, and the right edge specifies the sequence number immediately following the last sequence in the duplicate contiguous sequence. Fourth, if the D-SACK block reports a duplicate contiguous sequence from a, possibly larger, block of data in the receiver's data queue above the cumulative acknowledgement, then the second SACK block in that SACK option should specify that larger block of data. Fifth, following the SACK blocks described for reporting duplicate segments, additional SACK blocks can be used for reporting additional blocks of data, as specified in RFC 2018.

The document notes that because each duplicate segment is reported in only one ACK packet, information about that duplicate segment will be lost if that ACK packet is dropped in the network.
sections.plainLanguage: One duplicate per acknowledgement, and only the most recent one. If the duplicate sits inside a larger block of data the receiver already has, the block is listed second so the sender can still see it.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The guidelines are illustrated with six examples. In each of the first three, the data receiver has first received eight segments of 500 bytes each and has sent an acknowledgement with the cumulative acknowledgement field set to 4000, assuming the first sequence number is zero.

In Example 1, because several ACK packets are lost, the data sender retransmits packet 3000-3499, and the receiver subsequently receives a duplicate segment with sequence numbers 3000-3499. The receiver sends an acknowledgement with the cumulative acknowledgement field set to 4000, and the first, D-SACK block specifying sequence numbers 3000-3500.

In Example 2, following a lost data packet the receiver receives an out-of-order data segment, which triggers the SACK option as RFC 2018 specifies. Because of several lost ACK packets, the sender then retransmits a data packet. The receiver receives the duplicate packet and reports it in the first, D-SACK block, sending an acknowledgement with the cumulative acknowledgement set to 4000 and SACK blocks 3000-3500 and 4500-5000.

In Example 3, because of a lost data packet the receiver receives two out-of-order segments. It next receives a duplicate segment for one of these out-of-order segments, and sends an acknowledgement with the cumulative acknowledgement set to 4000 and SACK blocks 5000-5500 and 4500-5500.

Partial duplicate segments are covered separately. It may be possible that a sender transmits a packet that includes one or more duplicate sub-segments, that is, only part but not all of the transmitted packet has already arrived at the receiver. This can occur when the size of the sender's transmitted segments increases, which can occur when the PMTU increases in the middle of a TCP session. The guidelines apply to partial as well as full duplicate segments. When the SACK option is used for reporting partial duplicate segments, the first D-SACK block reports the first duplicate sub-segment; if the data packet being acknowledged contains multiple partial duplicate sub-segments, then only the first such duplicate sub-segment is reported.

In Example 4 the sender increases the packet size from 500 bytes to 1000 bytes. The receiver then receives a 1000-byte packet containing one 500-byte subsegment that has already been received and one that has not, and reports only the already received subsegment using a single D-SACK block. In Example 5 the sender increases its packet size to 1500 bytes, and the receiver receives a packet containing two non-contiguous duplicate 500-byte subsegments which are less than the cumulative acknowledgement field; the receiver reports the first such duplicate segment in a single D-SACK block. In Example 6 the same situation occurs above the cumulative acknowledgement field rather than below; the first, D-SACK block reports the first duplicate subsegment, and the second SACK block reports the larger block of non-contiguous data that it belongs to.
sections.plainLanguage: The document walks through six traces. The simple case is a segment the sender resent because acknowledgements were lost; the receiver names that segment in the first block. The harder cases are larger packets that partly overlap what the receiver already has.

sections.title: How D-SACK Meets PAWS
sections.content:
RFC 1323 specifies an algorithm for Protection Against Wrapped Sequence Numbers (PAWS). PAWS gives a method for distinguishing between sequence numbers for new data and sequence numbers from a previous cycle through the sequence number space. Duplicate segments might be detected by PAWS as belonging to a previous cycle through the sequence number space.

RFC 1323 specifies that for such packets, the receiver should send an acknowledgement in reply as specified in RFC 793, page 69, and drop the segment. Since PAWS still requires sending an ACK, there is no harmful interaction between PAWS and the use of D-SACK. The D-SACK block can be included in the SACK option of the ACK independently of the receiver's use of PAWS, and independently of the determination by PAWS of the validity or invalidity of the data segment.

TCP senders receiving D-SACK blocks should be aware that a segment reported as a duplicate segment could possibly have been from a prior cycle through the sequence number space. This is independent of the receiver's use of PAWS, and the document does not anticipate that this will present significant problems for senders using D-SACK information.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a separate TCP mechanism for spotting very old packets whose sequence numbers have wrapped around. The two do not clash, because that mechanism still sends an acknowledgement, and the D-SACK block can ride along in it.

sections.title: How a Sender Detects Duplicates
sections.content:
The extension enables the receiver to report the reception of duplicate data accurately. Because each receipt of a duplicate packet is reported in only one ACK packet, the loss of a single ACK can prevent the information from reaching the sender. The sender also cannot necessarily trust the receiver to send it accurate information.

For the sender to check that the first SACK block of an acknowledgement in fact acknowledges duplicate data, it should compare the sequence space in the first SACK block to the cumulative ACK carried in the same packet. If the SACK sequence space is less than this cumulative ACK, it indicates that the segment identified by the SACK block has been received more than once. An implementation MUST NOT compare the sequence space in the SACK block to the TCP state variable snd.una, which carries the total cumulative ACK, as this may give the wrong conclusion if ACK packets are reordered. If the sequence space in the first SACK block is greater than the cumulative ACK, the sender next compares it with the sequence space in the second SACK block, if there is one, which can determine if the first SACK block is reporting duplicate data that lies above the cumulative ACK.

TCP implementations which follow RFC 2581 could see duplicate packets in four situations. The document does not specify what action an implementation should take in these cases; the extension simply enables the sender to detect each of them, and it notes that later documents describe experimental proposals for sender responses.

The first situation is replication by the network. An ACK containing a D-SACK block which is lower than its ACK field and is not identical to a previously retransmitted segment is indicative of a replication by the network. Without D-SACK, the sender would not know that a packet had been replicated. The current SACK option already lets the sender identify duplicate ACKs that do not acknowledge new data, but D-SACK gives a stronger basis for that inference, which allows the sender to refrain from using those duplicate ACKs to infer packet loss or to send more data.

The second is a false retransmit due to reordering. If packets are reordered so that a segment arrives more than three packets out of order, TCP's Fast Retransmit algorithm retransmits the out-of-order packet. An ACK containing a SACK block lower than its ACK field and identical to a previously retransmitted segment is indicative of a significant reordering followed by an unnecessary retransmission. With D-SACK the sender knows that either the first transmission was delayed, or the first was dropped and the second was duplicated; given that no other segments have been duplicated, the second option can be considered unlikely. This allows the sender to adjust the duplicate acknowledgement threshold, to prevent such unnecessary Fast Retransmits in the future, and to undo an unnecessary reduction in the congestion window by resetting ssthresh to the value of the old congestion window and slow-starting until it reaches that point.

The third is a retransmit timeout due to ACK loss. If an entire window of ACKs is lost, a timeout results. The condition can be identified because the first ACK received following the timeout carries a D-SACK block indicating duplicate data was received. Without D-SACK the sender would be unable to decide that no data packet has been dropped, which for a TCP with some form of ACK congestion control would allow the return path to be controlled independently from the forward path.

The fourth is an early retransmit timeout, which occurs when the sender's RTO is too short and no packets have in fact been dropped. The first packet is retransmitted following the timeout, the original window then arrives at the receiver, and the retransmissions arrive afterwards, producing ACKs that carry SACK blocks identifying the duplicate segments. This can be identified because the ACK for byte 1000 is received after the timeout with no SACK information, followed by an ACK carrying SACK information indicating that the retransmitted segment had already been received. After determining that an unnecessary timeout has occurred, the sender could adjust the parameters for setting the RTO to prevent more of them.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender compares the first block of the SACK option with the cumulative acknowledgement in the same packet. If the block is behind it, that block names data the receiver already had, which tells the sender exactly what happened: the network duplicated a packet, or the sender resent something that had arrived.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document states that it neither strengthens nor weakens TCP's current security properties.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP's security is unchanged by this document. The document does note elsewhere that a sender cannot always trust what the receiver reports.

fields.name: Kind
fields.desc: Set to 5 for the SACK option.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: The length of the option, counting the kind and length octets.

fields.name: Left Edge of 1st Block
fields.desc: The first sequence number of the block of data received and queued.

fields.name: Right Edge of 1st Block
fields.desc: The sequence number immediately following the last sequence number of the block.

fields.name: Left Edge of nth Block
fields.desc: The first sequence number of the nth block of received data.

fields.name: Right Edge of nth Block
fields.desc: The sequence number immediately following the last sequence number of the nth block.

viz.caption: THE FIVE RULES FOR REPORTING A DUPLICATE (SECTION 4)

items.title: One duplicate per ACK
items.text: A D-SACK block only reports a duplicate contiguous sequence received in the most recent packet.

items.title: At most one D-SACK block
items.text: Each duplicate contiguous sequence is reported in at most one D-SACK block. Two identical blocks mean two duplicate segments arrived.

items.title: Edges of the duplicate
items.text: The left edge is the first sequence number of the duplicate and the right edge is the one immediately after its last.

items.title: The larger block goes second
items.text: If the duplicate sits in a larger block above the cumulative acknowledgement, the second SACK block names that larger block.

items.title: More blocks may follow
items.text: Further SACK blocks report additional blocks of data, as in RFC 2018.

viz.caption: THE FOUR SITUATIONS A SENDER CAN NOW TELL APART

cells: A D-SACK block lower than the ACK field that is not identical to a previously retransmitted segment.
A SACK block lower than the ACK field and identical to a previously retransmitted segment.
Retransmit timeout due to ACK loss
The first ACK after the timeout carries a D-SACK block showing duplicate data.
An ACK with no SACK information, followed by one whose SACK block names data already received.
